newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Russia, West disagree over NATO raid in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Russia, West disagree over NATO raid in Bosnia.

text.p: Russia joined Bosnian Serb leaders in condemning a NATO operation against war crimes suspects on Friday but Western envoys said the raid brought Bosnia closer to reconciliation and a more stable peace.
U.S. President Bill Clinton said the drive by NATO to arrest accused Bosnia war criminals was part of an overall attempt to salvage the Dayton peace accords.
"We basically believe that we have to make an effort to save the Dayton process," Clinton told reporters on Air Force One enroute to Denmark from Romania.
The Russian foreign ministry said the action by British special forces went beyond the NATO peacekeeping mandate and hinted Moscow might withdraw its soldiers from the operation.
"Such cowboy raids threaten the whole Dayton peace process, which is in any case going through a difficult period," the foreign ministry said in a statement.
Bosnian Serb leaders said the raid was an "irrational action" but stopped short of issuing threats against the 31,000-strong NATO-led force enforcing the peace accords.
The force said there were no reprisals against its troops after British special forces detained one suspect and shot dead another who opened fire when soldiers tried to arrest him.
The peace force declined to discuss the possibility of more arrests against those named by the U.N. war crimes tribunal.

NATO spokesman Major Chris Riley said Serb allegations that notorious police chief Simo Drljaca had been "murdered" were totally false. "Fire was returned in self-defence and as a result he was fatally wounded," Riley told reporters.
Clinton earlier defended the operation, in which American soldiers provided logistical support, saying it was "the right thing to do".
Serbs from the northwest Prijedor region held a protest on Friday and senior political and religious figures were expected to attend an elaborate funeral tentatively scheduled for Monday.

The NATO raid implied a shift in tactics. In the past, the alliance was reluctant to hunt down the 67 suspects on a published list who remain at large, such as former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic and his army commander Ratko Mladic.
They and others who believe they might be on a secret list of suspects now fear being grabbed at any time.
Momcilo Krajisnik, a senior Karadzic ally, underlined the concern aroused by the sealed indictments at a meeting with international civilian and NATO envoys.

"We must complain about the existence of some secret, private lists which are causing unease ... there must be no mystery about such lists because that would cause general panic," Krajisnik told reporters.
Western governments in recent months issued strong statements on the need to arrest war crimes suspects to allow for peacetime reconciliation among Bosnia's Serb, Moslem and Croat communities.
A United Nations spokesman said the raid bolstered the work of the tribunal in the Hague. Prosecutors had lobbied for a more robust approach for "a long, long time", Alex Ivanko said.
"That is why the tribunal is so hopeful that such operations will continue and all those indicted will end up in the Hague," Ivanko said.
The NATO swoop coincided with a power struggle in Serb territory between hardliners loyal to Karadzic and Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic.
Karadzic's allies accused Plavsic of provoking turmoil which they said NATO exploited to strike against the two suspects.
Patriarch Pavle, the highest authority in the Serbian Orthodox Christian church, planned to visit Bosnian Serb territory on Saturday to help repair relations between Plavsic and Karadzic loyalists.

The U.N. High Commissioner (UNHCR) praised the NATO action and noted that Friday was the second anniversary of the fall of the Srebrenica enclave, when thousands of Moslem men were executed or ambushed by Serb forces led by General Mladic.

"The fact that he (Mladic) and other indictees are still at large is an insult to the memory of their victims and an obstacle to the return of the survivors, who were driven from their homes in brutal waves of ethnic cleansing," spokesman Kris Janowski said.
